summary: Discusses how Forward Erasure Correction (FEC) coding and congestion control can work together. FEC adds redundancy to help with losses at the end of transfers or on networks with non-congestion loss, but it must not hide congestion signals. The memo offers guidance on letting both coexist. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Sending a few spare pieces lets the receiver rebuild lost ones. But the road might be jammed, so you must still slow down when it is crowded.

subtitle: How to add redundancy without breaking the network's congestion signals.

tldr.problem: Forward Erasure Correction adds spare data to recover lost packets, but if these spare packets hide the signs of network congestion from the congestion control mechanism, the sender may not slow down when the network is overloaded.
tldr.mechanism: FEC and congestion control must coexist as separate channels. The FEC layer sends redundancy but must allow the congestion control to see that losses occurred, even if FEC recovered them. Three placements are possible: FEC above transport, within it, or below it, each with different trade-offs.
tldr.outcome: When properly designed, FEC can recover from tail losses and non-congestion losses without harming fairness or hiding congestion. Poor designs may cause a coded flow to consume more than its fair share of bandwidth.

today: RFC 9265 is informational and represents consensus of the Coding for Efficient Network Communications Research Group. It remains a research topic; FEC has been deployed in real systems like RTP and emerging protocols such as QUIC, but the question of how to balance FEC with fair congestion control remains active.

sections.title: Why FEC and Congestion Control Must Work Together
sections.content:
Forward Erasure Correction (FEC) is a reliability technique distinct from retransmission. Instead of asking the sender to resend a lost packet, FEC includes spare repair packets in the stream. The receiver can use these to rebuild lost original packets without waiting. This is especially helpful at the end of short data transfers, where retransmission delays are long, and on networks with frequent non-congestion losses (such as lossy wireless links) that prevent the sender from using the link's full capacity.

Congestion control is the mechanism that makes TCP and other protocols fair and safe. It watches for signs of congestion—usually packet loss or ECN marks—and slows the sender's rate accordingly. This prevents the network from being overwhelmed.

The risk: FEC repairs losses, so it may hide congestion signals from the congestion control. If the sender does not realize congestion occurred because FEC hid the loss, the sender will not slow down, and the network suffers. This memo discusses how FEC and congestion control can coexist without this problem.
sections.plainLanguage: FEC is like sending the message twice to survive one lost copy. Congestion is like a traffic jam where everyone must slow down. If FEC hides the jam, everyone keeps going fast and crashes. So FEC must let congestion control see the jam.

sections.title: Treating FEC and Congestion Control as Separate Concerns
sections.content:
This memo frames FEC and congestion control as two separate channels inside a sender and receiver. The FEC channel carries original data packets and repair symbols from sender to receiver, and signals recovered symbols and loss information from receiver back to sender. The congestion control channel carries network packets (which may include source or repair symbols) and network signals such as acknowledgments and Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) marks.

Inside a host, these channels should be conceptually separate. The FEC layer decides its coding rate—how many repair symbols to send. The congestion control layer decides the sending rate based on network conditions. The key insight is that the inputs to each layer are distinct: the congestion controller does not need to know about recovered symbols, and the FEC coder does not need to see every ACK.

However, in practice, they must communicate. The congestion control must eventually see that a loss occurred—even if FEC recovered it—to adjust the sending rate. And the FEC coder needs feedback on which repair symbols were actually useful. This requires careful signaling between the layers.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of FEC as 'backup copies' and congestion control as 'slowdown when roads are jammed.' They are separate jobs, but someone must tell the road manager when a car was lost, even if a backup car arrived.

sections.title: Three Ways to Place FEC in a Protocol Stack
sections.content:
FEC above the transport: The application adds FEC on top of UDP or a partially reliable transport. Advantage: the FEC overhead does not consume the congestion window, so repair symbols do not contribute to congestion. Disadvantage: this only works if the transport does not guarantee in-order delivery; for TCP it is ineffective.

FEC within the transport: The transport protocol itself includes FEC. For example, QUIC could include FEC as part of its design. Advantage: FEC and congestion control can be jointly optimized; the sender can increase repair symbols while decreasing source symbols, keeping the total sending rate constant. Disadvantage: this requires changes to the transport protocol and may be complex to implement correctly.

FEC below the transport: FEC operates on the link between sender and receiver but below the transport layer, invisible to congestion control. Advantage: it works with any existing transport and can handle non-congestion losses on known lossy paths (like wireless). Disadvantage: repair symbols are not visible to the congestion controller, so losses may be hidden. This risks unfairness—the coded flow gets more bandwidth than non-coded flows because the congestion control thinks the network is uncongested.
sections.plainLanguage: Above: FEC helps before data reaches the road manager. Within: FEC and road manager work together. Below: FEC helps on the road but the road manager does not notice. Each has pros and cons.

sections.title: Trade-offs: Goodput, Latency, and Fairness
sections.content:
FEC has inherent trade-offs. Sending repair symbols uses bandwidth that could carry original data, reducing goodput (useful data delivered). Sending useless repair symbols—ones the receiver does not need—is wasteful. A well-designed FEC system adjusts the coding rate: send more repair symbols when losses are high or on short flows; send fewer when the network is clear.

FEC can improve latency by recovering tail losses faster than retransmission, but it adds delay from encoding and decoding. The gain depends on how often tail losses occur and how expensive retransmission is.

Fairness is the hardest issue. When FEC is placed below the transport, repair symbols add traffic without reducing the sending rate, so a coded flow may occupy more than its fair share of bandwidth. This harms non-coded flows sharing the same bottleneck. FEC above or within the transport can avoid this by ensuring that the total traffic—source plus repair—respects the congestion control rate.

The memo recommends that implementations use feedback from the receiver to adapt the coding rate, reducing useless repair symbols and improving efficiency.
sections.plainLanguage: Sending spares costs bandwidth. Too many spares waste capacity; too few lose data. Finding the right number depends on network conditions. And if your spares trick the network into giving you more space, other flows suffer.

sections.title: Research Questions and Design Recommendations
sections.content:
This memo identifies several open research questions. First, how should developers choose coding parameters dynamically based on the transport protocol and application requirements? Different protocols (TCP, SCTP, QUIC, etc.) and different application needs (real-time video, file download) suggest different coding strategies, but no standard method exists.

Second, should FEC mechanisms signal recovered packets to the congestion control, allowing the sender to know a loss occurred even though FEC recovered it? Some proposals already do this, but it needs further development.

Third, when should FEC be applied at different layers? For example, should FEC be applied only on the last mile (a noisy wireless link known to be lossy), or end-to-end? If only on the last mile, fairness concerns are reduced, but the design becomes more complex.

The memo recommends that researchers designing new FEC schemes should consider congestion control aspects and fairness, and should explicitly discuss trade-offs between hiding losses and improving throughput. When hiding a loss from congestion control, the author must justify why this is better than changing the congestion control algorithm itself to ignore some losses.
sections.plainLanguage: Open questions: How much spare data should you send? Should you tell the road manager about recovered losses? Where should FEC work? The memo recommends thinking about fairness, not just speed.
